meta.title: Security: what ai-jail protects and where it stops
meta.description: The ai-jail threat model in plain words: what the sandbox stops, what it cannot stop, which switches weaken it, how releases are built and how to report a flaw.

hero.title: A useful layer, with known edges
hero.lede: ai-jail keeps an AI coding agent away from your keys, your home directory and the rest of your machine. It is a process sandbox, so it shares your kernel. It does not replace a disposable virtual machine when the code is hostile.

stops.title: What it is built to stop
stops.lede: An agent can be talked into bad behavior by a web page, a package or a file in the repository. These are the things it then reaches for, and does not find.
stops.alt: The agent and the project sit inside a wall of bars. Six arrows leave the agent and bounce off the wall. Outside, dim and barred, are your home and keys, your shell secrets, the network, your screen and clipboard, your terminal and the jail policy.
stops.caption: The defaults. Every item on the outside stays there until you open it yourself.

items.text: Your home directory and the credentials in it. The agent gets a fresh, empty home, so ~/.ssh and ~/.aws do not exist in there.
Secrets in your shell. Environment variables are cut down to a small allowlist, so exported tokens stay outside.
The network. It is off, so nothing the agent reads can be sent anywhere. You can open it to a list of hosts, or all the way.
Host shared memory, your display server and your clipboard. Agent output passes through a filter that drops terminal clipboard and query sequences.
Typing into your terminal. Linux blocks the TIOCSTI call that fakes keystrokes, and macOS limits terminal control to the one terminal ai-jail created for the run.
Its own rules. A .ai-jail file inside a repository is untrusted: it can tighten the sandbox and never open it.

edge.title: Where the wall ends
edge.lede: The jail and your system stand on the same kernel. A bug in that kernel, in a driver or in the sandbox backend is a way around the wall, and ai-jail cannot do anything about it. A virtual machine brings its own kernel, which is why it is the stronger boundary.
edge.alt: On the left, your system and the ai-jail cage holding the agent stand on one shared slab, your kernel, and a dashed line runs from the agent through the slab to your system. On the right, a disposable VM encloses an agent standing on its own separate kernel.
edge.caption: A sandbox shares the ground with what it protects, and a VM brings its own.
items: Kernel and driver vulnerabilities. Every sandboxed process talks to the same kernel as the rest of your machine.
Bugs in your terminal emulator, above all with --terminal-passthrough, which turns the output filter off.
Defects in the sandbox backend itself: bubblewrap, Landlock and seccomp on Linux, sandbox-exec on macOS.
Secrets inside the project. A .env file in the repository is readable unless you mask it. See how to mask files.
Masks cover only paths that exist when the sandbox starts. A secret file created later, during the session, is not hidden.
Side channels and some classes of inter-process communication.
An allowed host is trusted wholesale. Allowing github.com with --allow-host lets the agent push to any repository there, not only yours.
Filtered egress is TCP only. There is no UDP, so a program that needs it does not work; it also cannot leak through it.

DNS under --allow-host. On Linux, name lookups inside the sandbox fail, so there is no DNS channel out. On macOS the system resolver is not fenced, so a low-bandwidth DNS channel remains, the same gap Anthropic documents for its own sandbox-runtime.
The proxy sees the host, the port and the timing of each connection. What travels inside stays between the two ends. How filtered egress is built.
On macOS, sandbox-exec is deprecated by Apple and is not equivalent to the Linux isolation. See the macOS differences.

callout.title: For code you believe is hostile, use a disposable VM
callout.text: ai-jail is for agents that are useful and sometimes wrong or misled. For malware analysis, or a repository you already distrust, start a virtual machine you can throw away. Compare the options.

switches.title: Switches that open the wall
switches.lede: Everything below is off until you turn it on, and most of them give the agent real access. How to set them is on the Configure page.

head.gives: What anything in the sandbox can then do

rows: Send anywhere everything it can read. Traffic is unrestricted. --allow-host is the tighter alternative.
Reach exactly the hosts you list, and their subdomains, over TCP through a built-in proxy. Each listed host is trusted wholesale.
Nothing new. This switch weakens nothing: it writes one line per launch to a file with mode 0600 outside the sandbox, so the agent never sees it.
Act as root on your machine through the Docker daemon.
Log keystrokes and take screenshots of other X11 windows.
Ask your systemd user manager to run services on the host.
Read your whole shell environment, secrets included. For API keys, --env-from-file passes one file instead.
Use the agent's saved login, for example Claude's ~/.claude.
Record and play audio while it is on.
See your real home directory. This is a broad exception; prefer a map of the one path you need.

closed.title: When in doubt, it refuses to start
closed.lede: A sandbox that silently starts weaker than you asked is worse than one that stops with an error. In these cases ai-jail stops.
items: A config file that exists and is invalid or unreadable.
A project .ai-jail that is a symlink. A symlinked global ~/.ai-jail is followed only to a regular file you own, that no one else can write, outside the project.
--lockdown when Landlock, the kernel's own filesystem rules, is missing, partial or fails to apply. --lockdown --no-landlock is rejected too.
--allow-tcp-port. That interface cannot constrain UDP, so the flag is accepted for compatibility, the launch fails, and the error points at --allow-host.
--network together with --allow-host, or --browser with --allow-host. The two contradict each other, so ai-jail refuses to launch.
An --env-from-file file that is a symlink, readable by its group or by everyone, owned by someone else or inside the project.
A BWRAP_BIN that points at a bubblewrap binary someone other than root could have replaced. It is ignored with a warning, and with no trusted bubblewrap the launch fails.

counter.title: Where it only warns
counter.text: Outside --lockdown, a Landlock failure is a warning. On a kernel too old for Landlock, ai-jail says so and continues with the bubblewrap layer alone. Read the startup lines.

checked.title: How the project is checked
checked.lede: One maintainer runs the project in the open. Below is what gets checked and what does not.

facts.label: sandbox-escape integration tests that try to write to /usr, read ~/.ssh, call ptrace and bpf, and expect to fail
unit tests in the source tree at version {version}
network requests at launch. The update check is opt-in with --update-check

audit.title: Audited internally, not by a third party
audit.text: Before 1.0 the project ran its own internal code audit and security review of the refactor, and published both in the repository. No outside firm has audited ai-jail. Read the security review.

release.title: How a release is made
items: Release tags are signed, and CI verifies each one against a key fingerprint pinned in the repository.
Every GitHub Action is pinned to a commit SHA, and actions are restricted to an allowlist.
Builds use a pinned Rust toolchain and --locked dependencies.
macOS binaries are signed and notarized by Apple.
Each archive ships with a SHA-256 checksum, and the publish job checks them again.

missing.title: What the release document says is still missing
items: Signing and publishing secrets are still stored at repository level and should move into the release environments.
No ruleset yet forces every v* tag to be signed.
Immutable releases are not enabled.
crates.io publishing still uses a token. Trusted publishing is planned.
With a single maintainer there is no second reviewer on changes or releases.

log.title: A log of what you allowed
log.text: --audit-log answers two questions: what did I let that agent do, and where did it try to reach. It appends one JSON line per launch, and with --allow-host on, one line per connection allowed or denied. It is off by default, and a project .ai-jail can only turn it off.

report.title: Report a vulnerability
report.text: Do not open a public issue. Use GitHub's private vulnerability reporting, include the steps to reproduce and the affected versions, and allow time to coordinate a fix.

items.a: The defaults are built and tested to block the ordinary routes: files, environment, network and host IPC. A kernel, driver, terminal or sandbox-backend bug could still let it out. Every process sandbox has that limit, which is why hostile code belongs in a disposable VM.

items.q: Is it safe to run with the network on?
items.a: It is safer than running the agent bare, because your keys and home directory are still not there to send. With --network, anything the agent can read, it can send. The middle ground is --allow-host: only the hosts you list are reachable, and each one is trusted as a whole. Mask the secrets inside the project first. See how to mask them.
Internally, before 1.0, with the reports published in the repository. It has had no third-party audit. The code is open under GPL 3.0, and private vulnerability reports are welcome.
